title: Diaries, Dialogues and Reviews
summary: Format and language features of diary entries, dialogues and reviews (of books, films or restaurants), with original examples and checklists.

notes.text: A **diary** is a private, personal record of events, thoughts and feelings. It is written in the **first person** ('I'), usually in the **past tense** for events and the present tense for current feelings, in an **informal**, honest tone.

items: Start with the **date** (and sometimes the time).
Describe what happened **and** how you felt about it, reflecting on events.
Usually 2 or 3 entries are written on different days to show how feelings change.

notes.title: Example diary entry (original)
notes.text:
Friday, 7 June

Dear Diary

I can't believe it. I forgot my lines in the middle of the school play! The whole hall went silent and all I could hear was my heart thumping. Then Kagiso whispered the next line from behind the curtain and somehow I carried on.

Afterwards, Mom hugged me and said nobody even noticed. I'm not sure that's true, but I feel a bit better. Tomorrow I'm going to thank Kagiso properly. Maybe I'll even try out for next year's play.

notes.title: Turning an event into a diary entry
notes.problem: Plain fact: 'I failed my maths test and did not tell my mother.' Rewrite it as the start of a diary entry.
steps: Add the date and a personal greeting: 'Monday, 4 March. Dear Diary,'
Use the first person and informal language.
notes.answer: 'Monday, 4 March. Dear Diary, today was awful. I got 32% for maths and I hid the test in my bag. I just couldn't face Mom.'

notes.text: A **dialogue** is a conversation between two or more people written in **script form** (like a play).

items: Give a short **context** at the top (who, where, what is happening).
Write the **speaker's name** on the left, followed by a **colon**.
Put **stage directions** (how something is said or done) in **brackets** in the present tense.
Start a new line for each speaker.
The conversation should sound natural and suit the characters and situation.

notes.title: Example dialogue (original)
notes.text:
[Context: Neo and his older sister Palesa are in the kitchen. Neo wants to borrow her laptop.]

NEO: (smiling sweetly) Palesa, you know you're my favourite sister?
PALESA: I'm your only sister. What do you want?
NEO: Just your laptop. For an hour. It's for a school project, I promise.
PALESA: (folding her arms) Last time it was 'for a school project', I found a game on my desktop.
NEO: That was research!
PALESA: (laughing) Fine. One hour. And you wash the dishes tonight.
NEO: Deal! (grabs the laptop and runs off)
A **review** gives a **personal, informed opinion** about a book, film, game, restaurant or event, to help others decide whether it is worth their time or money.

rows: Title of the work and often a rating (e.g. ★★★★☆)
Name, type (genre), author/director, main actors or place
What it is about, without giving away the ending (no spoilers)
Strengths and weaknesses with examples: characters, plot, acting, music, service, value for money
Your overall opinion and a recommendation: who would enjoy it?

notes.label: Language tip
notes.text: Use a variety of descriptive adjectives (gripping, predictable, hilarious, mouth-watering, overpriced) and justify every opinion with a reason or example.

notes.title: From opinion to review
notes.problem: 'The film was good.' Improve this sentence so that it works in a review.
steps: Give a reason or a detail.
Add a recommendation for the reader.
notes.answer: 'The film's fast-paced story and funny lead actor make it worth watching with friends.'

questions.prompt: In which person is a diary usually written?
Inverted commas are used around each character's words in a dialogue.
In a dialogue, in what are stage directions placed?
What is it called when a review gives away the ending of a story?
The main purpose of a review is to…
options: give an informed opinion and recommendation

questions.prompt: Match each feature to the text type.

pairs.left: Speaker's name followed by a colon

questions.prompt: In the example diary entry, how do the writer's feelings change from the beginning to the end?
questions.memo:
✓ At first embarrassed/panicked about forgetting lines (1)
✓ At the end relieved, grateful and even hopeful about next year (1)

questions.prompt: What does the dialogue reveal about Palesa's character?
questions.memo:
✓ She is suspicious / sensible (reminds Neo of the game) (1)
✓ but kind and humorous, as she agrees and laughs (1)

questions.prompt: Write a short dialogue (4 to 6 lines) between a learner and a teacher about a late assignment.
questions.memo:
✓ Context given (1)
✓ Correct format: names, colons, no inverted commas (1)
✓ At least one stage direction in brackets (1)
✓ Natural, suitable register for each speaker (1)

questions.prompt: Name THREE things that should be included in a film review.
questions.memo: Any three (1 each): title/genre/director/actors; brief summary without spoilers; strengths and weaknesses; rating; recommendation
